chapter_theme: The third part of the Valaik Kummi runs from the nets of desire and attachment through a string of animal riddles in the Siddhars' cipher (swan, tiger and parrots in the hall, cuckoo and owl, fish and honey, crow and eagle, crocodiles, bears and blind men, egg-laying birds, two moons on a chariot) to the Maiden seated in the triangle at the root. It then praises her as the one who kicked Death, drank the poison, burned the cities and killed Kamsa, who comes as mother, wife and sister, and asks whether Shakti or Siva is greater, answering with figures of mutual need: food and water, flesh and bone, earth and sky, woman and man. It closes on the worship that made the Siddhars, and on the claim that there is no deity above the Maiden and no song above this one.
structure_note: 1914 opens with the nets of desire and the burning house; 1915 to 1923 are animal and number riddles for the senses, the soul and death; 1924 to 1927 seat the Maiden in the root chakra and credit her with Siva's deeds; 1928 to 1930 give her kinship roles and the paradox of the barren mother; 1931 to 1935 pose and answer the question of Shakti against Siva; 1936 to 1938 end on worship, past merit and the song's self-praise.

1914.reading: That one is caught in the net of desire, that the house burned and perished at once, that the net of attachment came and covered it: for all this, praise the feet of the Lord, Maiden.
1914.nuance: The house that burns is the body of 1913; the two nets, ஆசை and பாசம், are the ordinary cause of its ruin. The remedy offered is devotion, not breath, which the song elsewhere prefers.

1915.reading: The swan is in the hall; a male tiger wanders there at play; five parrots still remain there, and three parrots reach out and catch them, Maiden.
1915.nuance: Cipher. Tradition reads the swan as the soul or the breath (hamsa), the tiger as the mind or death, the five parrots as the senses and the three that seize them as the three gunas or malas. The stanza is overlong by a foot and its line division is doubtful.

1916.reading: In the grove the cuckoo of the mango calls, and the new bridegroom comes to eat; the five-six owl sits deceiving in this way and stares; look at it, Maiden.
1916.nuance: Cipher. The bridegroom who comes to feed may be the soul entering the body, or the lover of the plain reading; அஞ்சாறு ஆந்தை (the five-six owl) is unexplained, perhaps the mind with its five senses and six faculties, which watches and deceives. The reading keeps to the surface.

1917.reading: There is a fish in the pool, and the kalasaval bird grazes on it and roams; there is honey in the field to eat, and it never cloys, Maiden.
1917.nuance: The honey that never cloys is the nectar of the head in the yogic reading; the fish and the bird that feeds on it are less clear, perhaps the breath and the mind, or the eye and its object. தூரணி and கலசாவல் are obscure words, the second perhaps a bird's name.

1918.reading: The crow sits on the branch, and the story lies in the strength; it is not far to see; this is knowledge, and if you look it shows, Maiden.
1918.nuance: The stanza says the secret is near and visible, which is the Siddhars' recurring claim; the crow on the branch is its figure, perhaps the mind on the body, the branch of 1906. கதை and தெம்பு rhyme with the first line and may be filler.

1919.reading: In the pond of the belly there is a hall; in Karuvur of that pond there is much mud; come with strength by the forest paths within, join them and examine, Maiden.
1919.nuance: Place-cipher as in 1912: கும்பி is the belly or the stomach, and Karuvur, a real town, is punned on கரு, the womb or embryo, so the muddy pond is the place of conception. The forest paths within are the channels.

1920.reading: Long ago, in the deep well two carp lay and showed off; the crow that stood watching them took fright, and the eagle killed it; look, Maiden.
1920.nuance: Cipher. Two carp in a well are the two eyes, or the sun and moon breaths; the crow is the mind that watches them and the eagle the breath or death that kills it. The parable is not explained and the reading is tradition's.

1921.reading: In the river there are five crocodiles; in the anthill two bears; Death is three blind men, and he takes with the noose, Maiden.
1921.nuance: The five crocodiles are the senses in the river of the body, the two bears perhaps the two deeds or desire and anger in the anthill (the body, or the root where the serpent sleeps), and the three blind men who are Death the three malas. பாசம் is both Yama's noose and the Saiva bond.

1922.reading: One bird lays an egg, and one bird spoils the egg; in the snare of circling Arur two deer struggle, Maiden.
1922.nuance: Cipher. The bird that lays and the bird that spoils may be the two breaths or the two deeds, the egg being the body (அண்டம்); ஆரூர் is a town-pun of uncertain target, and the two deer the soul and the mind in the snare of birth.

1923.reading: In the open ground of the eight great sky-circles, two moons stand on the chariot; they do not come and strike exactly, and the body has become red embers, Maiden.
1923.nuance: The two moons are the two eyes or the sun and moon breaths, on the chariot of the body (1900); அட்டமா விண்வட்டம் may be the eight directions of the sky or the eight centres. Their failure to strike together ends in the burning body of 1913.

1924.reading: Within the triangular round well, in the practice of the breath in the root mandala, in that cornered round chakra the Maiden sits, Maiden.
1924.nuance: The clearest doctrinal stanza of the chapter: the Maiden is seated in the triangle of the root centre, where tradition places the sleeping kundalini, and is reached by breath practice there. The riddles that precede it are, on the coded reading, about the same place.

1925.reading: On two legs there stands a tower; staying a long time, it will sink; when one sees it, the tower stands; the Maiden lets it neither be seen nor stand, Maiden.
1925.nuance: The tower on two legs is the body; the Maiden who neither lets it be seen truly nor lets it stand is the goddess as maya, the same power that seats herself at the root. The stanza gives her both the veil and the tower's fall.

1926.reading: Creating the five elements and joining them, creating the adharas, creating fond desire for women, the Maiden brings them together and fastens on Death, Maiden.
1926.nuance: Creation is hers, and so are desire and death: the goddess who makes the body also sets the trap that ends it. The stanza does not soften this; 1927 answers it by making her Death's conqueror too.

1927.reading: The Maiden is she who kicked Death with her foot, she who ate the halahala poison, she who created the undying world, she who demolished this human's fort.
1927.nuance: The kicking of Yama and the drinking of poison are Siva's deeds in the Saiva stories; the song gives them to the Maiden, as 1929 gives her Murugan's and Krishna's. மானுடன் கோட்டை இடித்தவள் recalls the burning fort of 1913: she builds and breaks the body-fort.

1928.reading: She came as mother and gave milk; she came as wife and gave pleasure; she became the supporting younger sister; for us she became the sister-in-law of desire and the mother-in-law.
1928.nuance: Every woman in a man's house is the goddess, which the kummi, sung by women, can say lightly. அமுதம் is milk here and also nectar; கொழுந்தி (wife's younger sister) is paired with ஆசை, which the stanza does not disown.

1929.reading: Smiling, she gently burned the cities; the Maiden kicked the Chetti of Senkadu; alone she conquered the Suras; single-handed she killed Kamsa.
1929.nuance: The burning of the three cities is Siva's, the conquest of the Suras Murugan's and the killing of Kamsa Krishna's; the goddess is made the agent of all. செங்காட்டுச் செட்டி is unclear: Yama kicked at Thirukkadaiyur is the likely story, but the name does not fit, and a merchant of Senkadu may be meant.

1930.reading: Such, you see, is her work; she is the barren one who never bore, the cruel one who is pregnant; you kohl-eyed women, listen: that young Maiden is the trident-bearer.
1930.nuance: ஈனா மலடி (the barren one who has not borne) and கொடுஞ்சூலி (the fierce pregnant one) are held together: she bears nothing and is always with child, the paradox of a creator without birth, as 1872 made her without parents.

1931.reading: Is the knife greater or the sheath? Is her eye greater or her face? Is Shakti greater or Siva? You tell me a little, Maiden.
1931.nuance: The question is posed with two homely pairs that cannot be ranked, knife and sheath, eye and face, and so is already answered: neither is greater. The song nevertheless returns to it (1967) and there decides for Siva.

1932.reading: It is not that food is greater and water not, and so with the Maiden being greater; it is not that gold is greater and silver not; I say it without lie, listen, you women.
1932.nuance: The syntax is loose; the sense taken is that the Maiden's greatness is like that of food beside water, each needed and neither above the other. A different reading makes food greater than water and so the Maiden greater than Siva; the gold and silver pair tells against it.

1933.reading: If it is flesh there is bone; take away the flesh and the shell of bone falls apart; the substance is Shakti in this way; play and dance the kummi.
1933.nuance: Flesh and bone answer the question of 1931 by a body: Shakti is the flesh that holds the bones, Siva the frame that falls without her. ஆமிசம் (substance, or flesh) is the pun that carries the claim.

1934.reading: Though what sprouted of old is the rice, if the husk is gone it will not grow: Avvai saw this and said it long ago; is it so or not, Maiden?
1934.nuance: The husk is the body, or maya, or Shakti: the soul-grain grows only inside it. The appeal to Avvai is to the proverb-poet, not to a known verse. The claim cuts against the ascetic use of the same image, in which the husk is the impurity to be removed.

1935.reading: Without earth there is no sky; without a little fragrance there is no flower; without woman there is no man; cherish this and see, Maiden.
1935.nuance: Three dependencies close the argument of 1931 to 1934: the goddess is the condition of the god, as earth of sky and scent of flower. The stanza reads as doctrine and as a women's song's plain boast.

1936.reading: In the pleasure garden there is light; for those who have ploughed the land there is paddy; to worship the Maiden wondrously, one needs what was left unfinished in a former life, Maiden.
1936.nuance: விட்ட குறை, the unfinished remainder, is the practice carried over from a past birth without which this worship cannot begin; the paddy for those who ploughed makes the same point. The Maiden's cult is a reward, not a starting point.

1937.reading: By worshipping the Maiden they became Siddhars; by firm desire for the Maiden they became the doers of Siva's work; they set the wage after looking at the work; will you know this manner, Maiden?
1937.nuance: சித்தர் ஆனார் is the song's account of what makes a Siddhar: worship of the Maiden, not alchemy or breath alone. கூலி, the wage set by the work, makes attainment proportional to practice, with no shortcut.

1938.reading: There is no deity above the Maiden; nothing guards honour better than the sari; there is no fortune above milk; and there is no song above the Maiden's kummi.
1938.nuance: A closing boast in four parallel lines; the sari and milk keep the stanza in the women's world of the kummi. The claim that no deity is above the Maiden is later qualified by the song itself (1967), which sets Siva higher.

links.note: Pattinathar's Puranamalai opens by confessing that he forgot his understanding by not praising the Maiden within the triangular chakra that rose at the root; Konganar says the Maiden sits in that cornered round chakra and is reached by breath in the root mandala. Both seat the Maiden in the root triangle, and the shared phrase shows a fixed Siddhar placement.

A later stanza of the same song says mother and wife are the same, for both gave, and asks whether raw fruit and ripe are equal; this stanza makes the Maiden mother, wife, sister and in-law in turn. The later stanza draws the moral the list implies: the goddess gives through every woman alike.

This stanza asks whether Shakti or Siva is greater and leaves the women to answer; the later stanza of the song answers that though the primal Maiden is great, she is not the master, and Siva is greater. The question posed as unanswerable is given an answer, against the drift of 1932 to 1935.

Tirumular says the three malas cover the soul as bran and husk cover the sprouting grain, and tells the reader to separate the bonds; Konganar, citing Avvai, says that rice without its husk will not sprout. Read with the husk as the body or maya in both, the claims conflict: for Tirumular the husk is what the soul must be freed from, for Konganar it is what the soul cannot grow without.

This stanza puts a saying in Avvai's mouth and asks whether it holds; the later stanza of the song says that whoever speaks what is apt and fits what is lacking, as Avvai did, is the guru. The appeal to Avvai is made general: the proverb-poet becomes the model of the teacher.

This stanza says there is no man without woman, as no sky without earth; the later stanza answers those who say a child comes from man and woman joining by saying the two joined became one seed without difference. The dependence of one on the other becomes their identity in the seed.

This stanza says there is no deity above the Maiden; the later stanza of the same song says that though the Maiden is great she is not the master, and Siva is greater. The two cannot both hold unless the Maiden of 1938 is Siva's own power rather than a rival deity; the song leaves the two claims standing.

source_issues: 1915 is overlong: its fourth line carries two refrains' worth of matter (எட்டிப் பிடிக்குமே மூன்று கிளியடி வாலைப்பெண்ணே) and the stanza may conflate two.
1917: தூரணி and கலசாவல் are obscure and may be corrupt.
1920, 1925 to 1930 and 1932 to 1933 lack the refrain வாலைப்பெண்ணே; 1929 and 1930 run on as one sentence.
